subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Calculate the mole fraction of H₂SO₄ in a solution containing 98% H₂SO₄ by mass.

verification.note: Unit 2 (Solutions) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.65-68, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. ARITHMETIC RECHECKED and the printed FINAL answer 0.9 is correct, but the line above it is not. BOOK SLOPPINESS (book p.65, VSAQ 11): the book rounds n(H₂O) = 2/18 to 0.1, writes the total moles as 1.1, and then prints "1/1.1 = 0.9". 1/1.1 is 0.909, not 0.9. Kept unrounded, 2/18 is exactly 1/9, the total is 10/9, and the mole fraction is exactly 9/10 = 0.900. This card carries the unrounded chain, so the printed answer and the working now agree.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Moles of each component
lines: 98% by mass means 98 g of H₂SO₄ in every
Molar mass of H₂SO₄ = 98 g mol⁻¹
Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹
steps.why: Percentage by mass is always measured against 100 g of solution, so taking 100 g as the basis turns the percentage straight into masses with no extra step. Both masses then divide by their molar masses, because a mole fraction is a ratio of moles and never of masses.
common_mistakes: Taking 98 g of acid in 100 g of WATER. Per cent by mass is per 100 g of solution, so the water here is only 2 g.
Rounding 2/18 to 0.1 at this stage. Keep 0.1111, because the rounding changes the third figure of the answer.
steps.memory_tip: 98% by mass: 98 g of acid and only 2 g of water in every 100 g of solution.
steps.margin_note: Write the basis line "take 100 g of solution" first. Both mole values are needed for this mark.

steps.label: The mole fraction
steps.why: The mole fraction is the moles of one component divided by the total moles of everything present. Kept unrounded the arithmetic is exact: 2/18 is 1/9, the total is 10/9, and 1 divided by 10/9 is 9/10. The book instead rounds to 1.1 and then prints 1/1.1 = 0.9; the printed answer is right but that division actually gives 0.909, so the rounding is what makes that printed line wrong, not the answer itself.
common_mistakes: Dividing by the moles of water instead of by the total moles. The denominator is the sum of all the components.
Leaving the answer with a unit. Mole fraction is a ratio of moles, so it has no unit.
steps.memory_tip: Denominator is the TOTAL moles, so the two mole fractions must add to 1.
steps.margin_note: Box 0.900 and write the check x(H₂O) = 0.100. The check costs one line and proves the denominator was right.

insider_note: Almost the whole mark is in reading the label: 98% by mass leaves only 2 g of water in 100 g of solution. Students who read it as 98 g in 100 g of water get about 0.15 and lose both marks.
